title: 9 Big Ideas within the Speaking and Listening Standards
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart answers a search query that keeps landing on his blog by synthesizing the CCSS Speaking and Listening anchor standards into nine big ideas, and the move he makes is to translate a policy document into classroom behaviors a teacher can actually run on Monday. His central claim is that listening is inseparable from speaking, and that a classroom which lets shy students stay in their shells is quietly writing them off. He offers his own practice as evidence: a year of refusing to coddle his shy freshmen ended with those students flourishing and thanking him. He then maps each big idea onto machinery most teachers already own - think-pair-share for partner talk, structured group work with real feedback, debates and speeches and index-card cold calls for whole-class talk - arguing that the standards ask for regularity and universality rather than novelty. He isolates 'productive' as the operative word in the anchor standards: college and career ready people add accurate and relevant information to a conversation. He also names his own recurring failure, discussions in which every student talks to the teacher and nobody talks to each other, and reframes the standards' real target as student-to-student exchange. He closes honestly, admitting he cannot decode the digital-media strand and inviting readers to argue with him.
points: Stuart's operative distinction is between speaking and listening: he argues you cannot be a competent speaker without being a competent listener, which makes listening a teachable object rather than a classroom management expectation.
His evidence against protecting shy students is experiential rather than theoretical - a year of requiring his shy freshmen to talk ended with those same students expressing sincere appreciation.
He reframes 'structured' group talk as a feedback problem: groups need to be shown what effective group talking looks like and given regular feedback on it, not merely seated together.

The keyword he pulls from the standards is 'productive' - CCR speakers add accurate and relevant information - which converts participation from a compliance grade into a content move that can be taught.

He names the failure mode of most teacher-led discussion, students addressing the teacher and ignoring each other, and identifies student-to-student response as what both the CCSS and real life actually require.
quotes: I love that we're talking about the Speaking and Listening standards rather than just the speaking standards. It is absolutely freaking certain that if you don't know how to listen, you don't really know how to speak, and you are not optimally prepared for college or career.

To you, this might be unforgivably obvious; but, alas, I have spent too many years enabling my shy students to remain in their shells and not insisting that they let me draw them way out. This last year, I didn't coddle my shy freshmen, and rather than shrivel up and die, they actually flourished, and by the end of the year many of them expressed sincere appreciation.

If you've been doing think-pair-share in your classes, you've got this covered. Pair shares are so old school but so darn money. Having students talk in pairs is a great way to let your students process and to let you walk around and check for understanding.

Whatever you do, just make sure that every kid is getting regular chances to talk to the whole class. The safer you make the classroom and the more regular you make these opportunities, the more efficacious shy kids tend to become.
A mega idea in the Speaking and Listening anchor standards is that college and career ready (CCR) people are productive members of conversations. Keyword: productive.

One major flaw of most class discussions I've led is this: students are all talking to me and ignoring each other. What the CCSS (and real life) call for is students actually talking with and responding to their peers.
